rows.prompt: Why orient a point
rows.outline: Opposite endpoint signs produce f(b)-f(a); all-positive points would produce a sum and would not telescope.

rows.prompt: What does the wedge remember
rows.outline: Swapping the ordered tangent edges reverses signed area, while ordinary area forgets that order.

rows.prompt: Why no 4-form in space
rows.outline: Four tangent inputs in R3 are linearly dependent; an alternating four-direction measurement is zero. The coordinate construction has only three distinct directions.

rows.prompt: Why two kinds of object
rows.outline: A vector is a displacement input; a covector is a linear scalar-valued measurement of that input. Coordinates alone do not identify their roles.

rows.prompt: What does the subscript carry
rows.outline: The base point selects the local measuring coefficients: e.g. wind/work depends on where the same velocity occurs.

rows.prompt: What does the dot product add
rows.outline: The inner product represents the linear functional by a vector; df exists without that metric choice. Different metrics change its representing gradient.

rows.prompt: What is the minus sign really saying
rows.outline: An ordered pair of edges determines orientation. Reversing that order negates the determinant and signed area.

rows.prompt: Why must a covector wedged with itself vanish
rows.outline: Two identical scalar measurements cannot distinguish two independent directed area coordinates: alpha(u)alpha(v)-alpha(v)alpha(u)=0.

rows.prompt: Why three basic 2-forms in space but only one in the plane
rows.outline: There are three distinct coordinate two-direction choices xy,yz,zx in R3, but just xy in R2; each gives a signed projected area.

rows.prompt: Why can't we add a line and an area
rows.outline: Homogeneous k-forms take k tangent inputs. A one-input and two-input measurement are not a single homogeneous form; the text is not claiming mixed-degree sums are impossible in a larger algebra.

rows.prompt: Why does space itself set a ceiling
rows.outline: Expand a coordinate (n+1)-fold wedge: one coordinate factor repeats, hence alternation makes each term zero. The checkpoint itself supplies this hint.

rows.prompt: What is the minus sign trying to tell us
rows.outline: Moving k ordered directions past l others entails kl adjacent swaps, each reversing orientation; total sign is (-1)^(kl).

rows.prompt: Why does the form move backward
rows.outline: First push tangent vectors by DT, then apply the target measurement. This defines a source covector, so forms travel from target to source.

rows.prompt: Where did the cross product come from
rows.outline: The three coordinate two-by-two minors are exactly the components of r_u cross r_v: both encode signed projected areas.

rows.prompt: What does the Jacobian's sign mean
rows.outline: A negative determinant means the parameter coordinate frame induces the opposite target orientation. Absolute area removes that sign; an oriented form retains it.

rows.prompt: Why a 1-form for a curve
rows.outline: Pulling back a 1-form produces one coefficient times dt, measuring one tangent velocity. A two-form pulls back to zero on a one-dimensional parameter interval.

rows.prompt: What is the integral really about
rows.outline: A compatible once-covering reparametrization changes the coefficient and the parameter increment by inverse compensating substitution factors. Curve substitution and surface change of variables provide the actual operation.

rows.prompt: Where does the minus sign come from
rows.outline: Changing a compatible oriented frame to the opposite one changes the evaluation of an alternating form by -1; ordinary unsigned area is a different integral.

rows.prompt: A rule, not a reading
rows.outline: dT_P is the whole linear map (a,b) maps to 3a-b/3; 7 is only its evaluation at (2,-3).

rows.prompt: Why does the gradient need a dot product
rows.outline: df is already a scalar-valued linear measurement; the dot product identifies its representing gradient vector.

rows.prompt: What if you double your speed
rows.outline: Linearity gives df(2v)=2df(v): same heading at twice the speed changes the reading twice as fast.

rows.prompt: Why a 2-form
rows.outline: The first circulation imbalance around a tiny rectangle is a signed area measurement (Q_x-P_y) dx wedge dy.

rows.prompt: Is curl really a new idea
rows.outline: The same exterior derivative has three signed-area coefficients in R3; the flux dictionary packages those coefficients as the curl vector.

rows.prompt: What is \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega saying
rows.outline: Add local circulation balances; each internal edge occurs in both directions, leaving the outer boundary.

rows.prompt: Why one operation, three names
rows.outline: The degree determines which classical dictionary applies: d on functions is df, on work forms is curl flux, and on flux forms is divergence volume.

rows.prompt: What does the balance really claim
rows.outline: Net outward crossing is total source density inside; internal crossings cancel in pairs.

rows.prompt: How can d\Phi=0 yet the flux be 4\pi
rows.outline: The form is undefined at the enclosed origin. Stokes/divergence cannot use that ball; a shell has outer 4pi and inner -4pi.

rows.prompt: Who does the cancelling
rows.outline: Equal mixed coefficients cancel because dy wedge dx=-dx wedge dy and repeated directions vanish. A symmetric product would add them.

rows.prompt: Why can't a hill make you spin
rows.outline: A global potential changes by endpoint difference, which is zero on a closed path; its C2 local curl is zero too.

rows.prompt: Algebra and geometry, same sentence
rows.outline: For sufficiently regular forms, Stokes applied twice relates integral of d² eta to the empty twice-boundary, both zero. This is a consistency interpretation, not an independent proof of arbitrary patching.

rows.prompt: Why is exactness the strong condition
rows.outline: A global primitive gives cancellation of mixed partials everywhere and zero relevant boundary integrals. Closedness only tests local coefficients and need not provide that primitive.

rows.prompt: What does the missing point actually break
rows.outline: The origin prevents a global single-valued angle. The unit-circle integral is 2pi, which rules out a global potential although the local coefficient derivative is zero.

rows.prompt: Local clue, global verdict
rows.outline: Local zero circulation cannot detect a noncontractible loop; the angle example gives the obstruction. The statement of the simply connected theorem supplies the positive implication, with GF-01 proof limitation.

rows.prompt: Why does the loop notice the hole
rows.outline: The circle cannot be filled/contracted through the omitted origin within this domain; locally zero curl coexists with its 2pi line integral.

rows.prompt: Where does the flux come from
rows.outline: The zero-source assertion is only away from the origin. On an admissible shell outer and inner flux cancel; the full ball is outside the theorem hypotheses.

rows.prompt: Two kinds of closed, one role for the hole
rows.outline: Closed form means derivative zero; closed geometric object means no boundary. Zero integral requires a filling in the domain (or exactness), not just these two unrelated adjectives.

rows.prompt: Why does the hole turn the other way
rows.outline: Keep the region on the left; walking the inner hole clockwise does that.

rows.prompt: What does forced mean here
rows.outline: Changing only the boundary traversal negates one side of Stokes. The selected normal induces the compatible traversal.

rows.prompt: What is the boundary of a boundary
rows.outline: Each box edge occurs twice with opposite induced directions, so the oriented chain cancels.

rows.prompt: One degree less
rows.outline: The boundary is k-1 dimensional, so it accepts a (k-1)-form.

rows.prompt: Why raise the degree
rows.outline: d converts the boundary measurement into its interior k-dimensional density.

rows.prompt: Where did the inside go
rows.outline: Adjacent regions traverse a shared edge oppositely and contribute equal negative integrals.

rows.prompt: Where does the minus sign come from
rows.outline: The positively traversed interval enters at a and exits at b, hence signed boundary b-a.

rows.prompt: Why do interior points cancel
rows.outline: Interior partition points are an exit of one interval and entry of the next; their function values cancel.

rows.prompt: Why call it a boundary theorem
rows.outline: The total derivative integral is endpoint data f(b)-f(a), an oriented boundary measurement.

rows.prompt: What does the coefficient measure
rows.outline: Q_x-P_y is infinitesimal counterclockwise circulation per unit signed area.

rows.prompt: Why does the hole turn the other way
rows.outline: Changing the inner direction adds its area instead of subtracting the hole, breaking Stokes.

rows.prompt: One theorem wearing two costumes
rows.outline: Use either the work form P dx+Q dy or the flux form P dy-Q dx; d computes curl or divergence accordingly.

rows.prompt: Why does curl show up at all
rows.outline: Expanding d(P dx+Q dy+R dz) with antisymmetry produces exactly the three curl coefficients.

rows.prompt: What does “only sees the boundary” mean
rows.outline: For this exact 2-form d omega, all admissible surfaces induce the same boundary integral; arbitrary 2-forms need not.

rows.prompt: How can one point matter
rows.outline: The chosen spanning disk includes a point where the form is undefined, so its hypotheses fail.

rows.prompt: Why does the degree go up
rows.outline: Boundary flux is measured on a surface; total source density is measured in the enclosed volume.

rows.prompt: What is the boundary "remembering"
rows.outline: Only net crossing remains after internal transfers cancel; the boundary integral equals total divergence.

rows.prompt: Why must a curl's flux cancel
rows.outline: d(d omega)=0 for C2 coefficients, so Stokes on the solid gives zero closed-surface flux.

rows.prompt: Why does the inside disappear
rows.outline: Each shared edge carries opposite induced orientations, so its two integrals cancel.

rows.prompt: From local to global
rows.outline: Add exact rectangle identities and cancel shared edges; general curved-domain limiting is separately an outline.

rows.prompt: Why are the twins twins
rows.outline: Apply Stokes twice at the appropriate degrees: the twice boundary cancels, and the integral of d² is zero.

rows.prompt: Why subtract at one end
rows.outline: Outward/end signs are b-a and recover the endpoint difference, not a sum.

rows.prompt: Why a 2-form here
rows.outline: The boundary of a solid is two-dimensional and measures two tangent directions.

rows.prompt: One theorem, four faces
rows.outline: Dimensions 1,2,2-in-space,3 and the work/flux dictionaries yield FTC, Green, classical Stokes, divergence.

rows.prompt: Which line actually changed
rows.outline: Only the clockwise line integral was negated; the fixed positively oriented square integral remained 1.

rows.prompt: If d\alpha=0, why isn't the loop integral zero
rows.outline: The field is defined only on a punctured domain; the disk needed by the careless step is inadmissible.

rows.prompt: Where did the missing -2 come from
rows.outline: H has a jump at y=0, so d omega is not defined there in the C1 calculus; the missing internal interface contribution is -2.

rows.outline: For S=-sum p_i log p_i, gradient components=-(log p_i+1); Hessian diagonal=-1/p_i. On any nonzero feasible segment its second derivative is negative, so an interior stationary point is the unique global maximum, with continuity 0log0=0 handling boundary comparison as explained locally. Normalization alone gives p_i=1/n, S=log n. For energies(0,1,2) and0<U<2, two independent constraint gradients(1,1,1),(0,1,2) satisfy Ch9 two-constraint hypotheses. Lagrange gives p=C(1,q,q²),q=exp(-beta)>0,C=1/(1+q+q²). U(q)=(q+2q²)/(1+q+q²) has derivative(q²+4q+1)/(1+q+q²)²>0 and limits0,2, so a unique positive q exists by IVT. U=1/2 gives q=(-1+sqrt13)/6 and those probabilities. EndpointU require a point mass, not finite beta.
